intro: We use comparatives to compare two people, things or situations: “bigger than”, “more expensive than”. The form depends on the length of the adjective: -er for short words, more for long words.
objectifs: Form comparatives of short adjectives (-er) and long adjectives (more).
Use the spelling rules and know the irregular forms (better, worse, further).
Use than and less … than, and modify comparatives with much, a lot, a bit, far.
Avoid typical mistakes: “more bigger”, “more good”, “that” instead of “than”.

texte: For a one-syllable adjective, add -er, then “than” before the thing you compare: cheap → cheaper than, old → older than, fast → faster than.
Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y follow the same rule, but y changes to i: easy → easier, happy → happier, busy → busier.

lignes: ends in -w, -x, or -y after a vowel: no doubling

exemples: This bag is cheaper than that one.

texte: For two-syllable adjectives that do not end in -y, and for all adjectives with three or more syllables, put “more” before the adjective. The adjective does not change.

A few two-syllable adjectives can take both forms: quiet (quieter / more quiet), simple, narrow, clever, polite. With these words, “more” is rarely wrong, but the -er form often sounds more natural for quiet, simple, narrow and clever.
exemples: English is more useful than Latin for my job.
The train is more comfortable than the bus.
This exercise is more difficult than the first one.

texte: Some very common adjectives (and adverbs) are irregular. Learn them by heart: you will use them all the time.
“Further” and “farther” both mean “more far” for distance; “further” is more common in British English, and only “further” also means “more, extra” (further information).

lignes: Your English is better than mine.
Kribi is further than Limbé from Douala.
I have more work this week.

texte: “Than” introduces the second part of the comparison. Do not confuse it with “that” or with “then” (after that).
After than, we usually use an object pronoun: “She's taller than me”. “Taller than I am” is more careful; “taller than I” alone sounds very formal.

For the opposite idea, use “less + adjective + than”, especially with long adjectives: less expensive, less important. With short adjectives, “not as … as” (lesson 66) is more natural: “not as old as” rather than “less old than”.
exemples: My brother is older than me.
This hotel is less expensive than the one in Brussels.
You work harder than I do.

sections.titre: Making a comparison stronger or weaker
texte: For a big difference, put much, a lot or far before the comparative. For a small difference, use a bit, a little or slightly. Never say “very bigger”.
To show a change over time, repeat the comparative with and: “bigger and bigger”, “more and more expensive”.
exemples: Montreal is much colder than Paris in winter.
The new phone is a bit more expensive.
Rent is getting more and more expensive.

formule: short adjective + -er + than · more + long adjective + than · (much / a bit) + comparative
prononciation: The -er ending is /ə/ in British English: bigger /ˈbɪɡə/, cheaper /ˈtʃiːpə/; in American English the final r is pronounced /ər/.
“than” is almost always weak: /ðən/: taller than me /ˈtɔːlə ðən miː/.
The th in “than” is voiced /ð/, with your tongue between your teeth: not “zan” or “dan”.
“better” is /ˈbetə/ (UK); in American English the tt sounds like a quick d /ˈbedər/.
erreurs: She is more tall than me.
My car is more good than yours.
My car is better than yours.
In comparisons, use than, not that.
Before a comparative: much / a lot / far, not very.

dialogue.contexte: Nadia can't choose between two flats in Montreal. She talks to her friend Thomas.
lignes: So, which flat do you prefer?
The one on Rue Saint-Denis is bigger and brighter than the other one.
Yes, a bit. It's 100 dollars more a month.
It's cheaper and closer to my office, but it's much smaller and noisier.
Hmm. A quieter flat is better for your sleep.
You're right. Sleep is more important than money!

mots: Rent is more expensive in Paris.
making you feel relaxed and pleasant
The village is quieter than the city.
Our street is noisier at night.
It's safer to take a taxi at night.
The metro is more crowded in the morning.
My office is closer to the station.
This room is brighter than the kitchen.
to look at how things are similar or different

exercices.consigne: Complete with the comparative of the adjective and than.
items: My new job is ___ (good) my old one.
Winter in Canada is ___ (cold) winter in Belgium.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the word in brackets in the right place.
items: Paris is much bigger than Lyon.
This test was a bit easier.
Prices are getting high. (a change over time)
Prices are getting higher and higher.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: My sister is more young than me.
My sister is younger than me.
This film is more better than the book.
This film is better than the book.
The traffic is very worse today.
The traffic is much worse today.

exercices.consigne: Use the words to write a full sentence.
items: My house is smaller than yours.
Is French more difficult than English?
this hotel / less / expensive / the other one
This hotel is less expensive than the other one.

exercices.consigne: Compare two cities you know in five sentences (size, prices, weather, atmosphere…).
items: Douala is bigger and busier than Buea. Buea is much cooler because it's near Mount Cameroon. Life is a bit cheaper in Buea. Douala is noisier, but the nightlife is more exciting. For me, Buea is more relaxing.

a_retenir: Short adjective: -er + than (cheaper than); long adjective: more + adjective + than.
Spelling: big → bigger, easy → easier, nice → nicer.
Irregular: good → better, bad → worse, far → further / farther.
Never “more better”, never “very + comparative”: much / a lot / a bit + comparative.
Use than (not that); after than: me, him, her… or subject + helper verb (than I do).
